questiontext.text: A graph is bipartite if and only if:

answer.text: Its vertices can be 2-colored so that no edge joins two same-colored vertices

feedback.text: Correct — a proper 2-coloring is exactly bipartiteness.

answer.text: It is connected and has no isolated vertices

feedback.text: No — connectivity is unrelated to bipartiteness.
No — that is the Eulerian condition, not bipartiteness.

answer.text: It contains at least one cycle

feedback.text: No — a tree (no cycles) is bipartite; cycles are not required.

generalfeedback.text: A graph is bipartite exactly when its vertices split into two sets with all edges crossing between the sets — equivalently, a proper 2-coloring exists.

questiontext.text: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of which length?

feedback.text: Correct — bipartite graphs have no odd cycles.
No — even cycles are perfectly fine in bipartite graphs.
No — every odd cycle (5, 7, ...) is forbidden, not just triangles.
No — even cycles are allowed; only odd ones are forbidden.

generalfeedback.text: An odd cycle cannot be 2-colored, so it is the exact obstruction: bipartite ⟺ no odd-length cycle.

questiontext.text: Which traversal-based method decides whether a graph is bipartite?

answer.text: BFS/DFS 2-coloring: color each vertex opposite to its parent and check for conflicts

feedback.text: Correct — alternate colors along the traversal and detect a clash.
No — topological sort applies to DAGs and does not test bipartiteness.

answer.text: Run Dijkstra and check for negative edges

feedback.text: No — that is unrelated to 2-colorability.

answer.text: Count the vertices and check it is even

feedback.text: No — parity of |V| says nothing about bipartiteness.

generalfeedback.text: BFS or DFS assigns alternating colors; if any edge connects two vertices that receive the same color, an odd cycle exists and the graph is not bipartite.

questiontext.text: Using adjacency lists, the BFS/DFS bipartite check runs in time:

feedback.text: Correct — a single linear traversal suffices.
That would be the adjacency-matrix bound, not adjacency lists.
No — you do not try all colorings; one traversal decides it.
No — no sorting or priority queue is used.

generalfeedback.text: The 2-coloring is done in one BFS/DFS pass, examining each vertex and edge a constant number of times — O(V + E).

feedback.text: Correct — a tree has no cycles, hence no odd cycle, so it is bipartite.
Trees have no cycles at all, so certainly no odd cycle; they are bipartite.

questiontext.text: A single cycle of length 5 (C₅) is bipartite.

feedback.text: No — a 5-cycle is an odd cycle and cannot be 2-colored.
Correct — an odd cycle is not bipartite.

questiontext.text: A graph fails to be bipartite exactly when it contains an ______-length cycle (fill in the English word).

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about bipartite graphs are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: A bipartite graph can be properly colored with just 2 colors

feedback.text: Yes — 2-colorability is the definition.

answer.text: Bipartiteness can be tested in O(V + E) time

feedback.text: Yes — a single BFS/DFS 2-coloring pass does it.

answer.text: Every bipartite graph must contain a cycle

feedback.text: No — trees are bipartite and acyclic.

answer.text: A graph with an odd cycle can still be bipartite

feedback.text: No — an odd cycle makes 2-coloring impossible.

generalfeedback.text: Bipartite means 2-colorable, equivalently no odd cycle, testable in O(V + E). Cycles are not required, and any odd cycle rules out bipartiteness.
